extracted.intended_audience: researchers and social scientists interested in methods for resolving contested empirical disagreements
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing and assessing adversarial collaborations: studies co-designed by intellectual opponents with pre-agreed analysis, neutral collaborators, and pre-specified predictions/interpretation rules to reduce epistemic impasses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversarial collaboration (overall concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual opponents co-design new studies to get beyond entrenched opposing camps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The idea is that intellectual opponents co-design new studies. As much as possible, they should agree ahead of time about how the data will be analyzed, and include other neutral collaborators. Then they write down their predictions, their uncertainties, and how different results will change their opinion. When the study is done, hopefully they end up agreeing about how to interpret it. But even if they didn’t, examining such a study, including the collaborators’ predictions beforehand, would really help other people decide what to believe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-agreement on data analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Agree ahead of time about how the data will be analyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specifying analysis reduces post-hoc interpretation disputes. The post recommends that, 'as much as possible, they should agree ahead of time about how the data will be analyzed' so that results cannot be selectively interpreted to favor prior positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include neutral collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: Include neutral collaborators in the study team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral collaborators are recommended alongside opposing parties to help design and interpret the study fairly and increase credibility of the process and findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify predictions, uncertainties, and decision rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down predictions, uncertainties, and how different results will change opinions before data collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documenting predictions and how results would change views provides transparency and helps outside readers evaluate the evidentiary weight of outcomes. The blog emphasizes writing down 'their predictions, their uncertainties, and how different results will change their opinion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility conditions for adversarial collaboration (when it's most feasible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration is most feasible when clashing camps have advanced testable theories, subscribe to common canons for testing, and disagreements are robust but respectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tetlock calls such communities 'epistemic Heaven.' In these contexts adversarial collaboration may be unnecessary because theory-testing conditions are already good, but feasibility is high when there are clear testable theories and shared methodological standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infeasibility / political unattractiveness (when it's least feasible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adversarial collaboration is least feasible when the scientific community lacks clear falsification criteria, disagrees on key methodological issues, relies on second- or third-best substitute methods for testing causality, and is fractured into opposing camps that engage in ad hominem posturing and have intimate ties to political actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tetlock calls this situation 'epistemic hell.' The post warns that 'what makes adversarial collaboration scientifically attractive—the prospect of breaking epistemic impasses—may also render it politically unattractive' because parties might prefer ambiguity. Failures to broker collaborations in such settings are informative about politicization of the debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target topics in the 'murky middle' (where expected returns are greatest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus adversarial collaborations on topics in the 'murky middle' where theory-testing conditions are less than ideal but not hopeless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tetlock argues that if collaboration is unnecessary in epistemic heaven and impossible in epistemic hell, then the greatest expected returns come from the 'murky middle' — areas where tests can be designed but conditions are imperfect. The post invites suggestions for topics that could benefit from such collaborations.
